q: A needle roller bearing fitted in workshop machinery is a bearing in which:

options.A: The rollers are long in proportion to their very small diameter, so that the bearing carries a heavy load where radial space around the shaft is very limited
options.B: The rolling elements are balls running between grooved races, suited mainly to high speeds and light loads
options.C: The rollers are barrel-shaped so that the bearing can take up misalignment of the shaft by itself
options.D: The rolling elements are short cylinders of the same length as their diameter, used for very heavy slow shafts

q: A plummer block, as used for supporting the shafts of workshop machinery, is:

options.A: A solid block of cast iron in which a plain hole is bored to receive the shaft directly
options.B: A ring fitted round a shaft to stop oil from travelling along it out of a bearing
options.C: A bracket which carries the two ends of a countershaft and is hung from the ceiling of the shop
options.D: A split pedestal housing, bolted down to its base, which supports a journal bearing and whose top half can be removed for fitting or inspection

q: An Oldham coupling, as used to join two shafts in a workshop machine drive, is:

options.A: A pair of flanges keyed to the shaft ends and bolted rigidly together face to face
options.B: A three-piece coupling whose middle disc engages slots in the two end discs, letting it join shafts whose axes are parallel but slightly out of line
options.C: A coupling in which the torque is passed from one shaft to the other through a body of oil set in motion by vanes
options.D: A coupling made of a short length of stiff rubber hose clamped to the two shaft ends

q: A universal joint, as used in the drives of workshop machines and equipment, is a joint which:

options.A: Transmits rotary motion between two shafts whose axes meet at an angle, and keeps working as that angle changes
options.B: Joins two shafts end to end in a straight line and can be parted by sliding one half along the shaft
options.C: Connects a shaft to its pulley and slips whenever the load becomes excessive
options.D: Allows a shaft to be engaged with or freed from its drive while both are running, by means of friction faces

q: A timing belt used in the drives of workshop machines is:

options.A: A flat leather belt joined by a laced fastener and run over crowned pulleys
options.B: A belt of wedge-shaped section which drives by friction in the grooves of its pulleys
options.C: A belt with teeth formed on its inner face which engage matching toothed pulleys, giving a positive drive without slip so that the driven shaft keeps in step with the driver
options.D: A drive made of several ropes running side by side in the grooves of a large pulley

q: A feather key, as used in assembling a pulley or gear on a shaft in a workshop, is:

options.A: A segment-shaped key which sits in a curved slot milled in the shaft and rocks in its seating
options.B: A key with a raised head at one end by which it can be drawn out of its keyway with a wedge
options.C: A key which rests on the surface of the shaft in a shallow seating and drives by friction alone
options.D: A parallel key fastened to one member so that the mating member can slide axially along the shaft while still being driven by it, as in a sliding-gear drive

q: A taper turning attachment fitted to a centre lathe in a workshop serves to:

options.A: Turn short steep tapers by swivelling the compound slide to the taper angle and feeding the tool by hand
options.B: Guide the tool along a bar set at the required taper angle while the carriage moves straight, so that long tapers can be turned without setting over the tailstock
options.C: Produce a taper by using a broad tool whose cutting edge is shaped to the taper required
options.D: Hold a long tapered workpiece between the centres while it is being ground to size

q: The feed rod fitted along the bed of a centre lathe in a workshop is:

options.A: The threaded rod which is used only for cutting screw threads on the workpiece
options.B: The rod by which the speed of the spindle is changed from the headstock levers
options.C: The smooth rod running along the lathe bed which drives the carriage and cross-slide for ordinary turning and facing feeds, thread cutting being left to the lead screw
options.D: The rod which carries the change gears at the end of the headstock

q: A ball screw, as used for the feed drives of precision and numerically controlled machines in a workshop, is:

options.A: A screw-and-nut feed drive in which steel balls recirculate between the screw and the nut, giving a smooth and accurate feed with very little friction and backlash
options.B: A screw whose thread is of square section and which is used for the vice and press screws of the shop
options.C: A screw fitted with a ball handle by which the slide of a machine is fed by hand
options.D: A worm which drives a large wheel and gives a very slow feed to a machine table

q: Arc blow, as the term is used in arc welding in a workshop, is:

options.A: The forcing of molten slag into the body of a weld, where it remains trapped on cooling
options.B: The failure of the weld metal to join properly with the parent metal at the edges of the joint
options.C: The running back of the welding flame into the blowpipe, marked by a sharp report
options.D: The deflection of the welding arc from its intended path by magnetic forces, which disturbs the deposition of the weld metal

q: A crater, as the term is used for a welded joint made in a workshop, is:

options.A: The groove melted into the parent metal along the edge of a weld, left unfilled by weld metal
options.B: The unfilled depression formed at the end of a weld run where the arc is broken, which is a common seat of cracks
options.C: The raised portion of weld metal standing above the surface of the plates joined
options.D: The line along which two runs of weld metal meet in a wide woven bead

q: A butt joint, as made in the fabrication work of a workshop, is a joint in which:

options.A: The two members lie edge to edge in the same plane and are welded along the meeting edges
options.B: One member lies over the edge of the other and the two are welded along the overlapping edges
options.C: The end of one member is set against the face of the other so that the joint is shaped like a letter of the alphabet
options.D: The edges of the two members are bent up and folded together before welding

q: Austempering of a steel component in the heat treatment shop of a workshop is a treatment in which the component is:

options.A: Quenched into a hot bath and held there only until its temperature is even throughout, then cooled in air and tempered
options.B: Cooled slowly in air after heating, so that a fine pearlitic structure is obtained for wire to be drawn further
options.C: Heated and quenched into a hot bath, then held in the bath until its internal structure has changed fully to bainite before it is cooled to room temperature
options.D: Quenched in oil or water in the ordinary way and then reheated to a lower temperature to remove brittleness

q: Spheroidising of a hard steel component in a workshop is a heat treatment in which:

options.A: The component is heated and cooled repeatedly so that its grain is refined throughout
options.B: Internal stresses set up by welding or machining are removed by heating without changing the structure of the steel
options.C: Carbon and nitrogen are absorbed into the surface of the component to form a hard case over a tough core
options.D: The carbide in the steel is made to gather into small rounded globules by prolonged heating, leaving the steel soft and easy to machine

q: The hardenability of a steel, as the term is used in the heat treatment work of a workshop, means:

options.A: The resistance of the surface of the steel to indentation by a hardened ball or point
options.B: The property which governs the depth to which the steel will harden when quenched, as distinct from the surface hardness it can reach
options.C: The ability of the steel to absorb energy and resist fracture under a sudden blow
options.D: The increase in hardness which a steel shows after it has been heavily cold worked

q: In the scleroscope hardness test carried out on workshop materials, the hardness is judged from:

options.A: The height to which a small diamond-tipped hammer rebounds after falling on the surface of the specimen
options.B: The diameter of the impression left by a hardened steel ball pressed into the surface under a standard load
options.C: The depth to which a cone or ball penetrates the surface under a minor load followed by a major load
options.D: The size of the impression left by a square-based diamond pyramid pressed into the polished surface

q: Bluing of a steel article in the finishing shops of a workshop consists of:

options.A: Coating the article with zinc by dipping it in a bath of the molten metal
options.B: Depositing a layer of phosphate crystals on the article to form a base for paint
options.C: Producing a thin blue-black oxide film on the article by heating or by chemical treatment, giving it a neat finish and slight protection against rust
options.D: Covering the article with a dry powder which is then baked on it to form a hard coat

q: Passivation of a stainless steel article in a workshop consists of:

options.A: Immersing the article in acid to remove mill scale and fire scale before it is painted
options.B: Treating the article in an acid bath so that surface contamination is removed and its protective oxide film is restored, recovering its resistance to corrosion
options.C: Washing the article in a hot alkaline solution to remove oil and grease before assembly
options.D: Heating the article in a furnace until a thick black scale forms over its whole surface

q: Embossing, as carried out on a press in the press shop of a workshop, is an operation in which:

options.A: A blank of the required outline is cut out of sheet metal by a punch and die
options.B: The sheet is squeezed in closed dies so that sharp impressions are formed on both its faces and its thickness is changed
options.C: The sheet is drawn down into a die cavity so that a hollow article of depth is formed from it
options.D: A design or lettering is raised in relief on sheet metal between matching dies, the thickness of the sheet remaining much the same

q: Hemming, as carried out in the sheet-metal work of a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Folding the edge of a sheet-metal article back on itself so that the edge is stiffened and is no longer sharp
options.B: Joining the edges of two sheets by folding them together and flattening the fold down
options.C: Bending the edge of a sheet outwards at an angle so that it can be riveted to another part
options.D: Rolling the edge of a sheet round a wire so that it forms a rounded bead along the edge

q: A castle nut, as used in the assemblies of a workshop, is a nut:

options.A: Whose top is closed by a dome so that the end of the bolt is covered and protected
options.B: Which is made long so that the threaded ends of two rods can be joined end to end in it
options.C: Whose top is slotted like the battlements of a castle, so that a split pin passed through the slots and the bolt locks the nut against slackening
options.D: Which has a collar of fibre or plastic let into it so that it grips the bolt and resists slackening

q: A wing nut, as used on the equipment and assemblies of a workshop, is a nut:

options.A: Which is turned by a spanner engaging flats formed on its outside like those of an ordinary nut
options.B: Provided with projecting wings which are gripped between the fingers, so that it can be tightened or slackened by hand without any spanner
options.C: Provided with a ring at its top through which a lifting sling can be passed
options.D: Which is left plain and round and is tightened by means of a hook spanner engaging holes in its face

q: A foundation bolt, as used in the installation of machines in a workshop, is a bolt:

options.A: Fitted through the feet of a machine into holes drilled in a wooden packing piece under the machine
options.B: Screwed into a tapped hole in the bed of the machine itself to hold down a fixture
options.C: Passed through two flanges of a machine and secured by a nut at its lower end
options.D: Built into the concrete foundation of a machine, its projecting threaded end receiving a nut which holds the machine firmly on its foundation

q: A taper pin, as used in the assembly work of a workshop, is a pin:

options.A: Tapered along its length, driven into a matching tapered hole so that it fastens and locates two parts together and can be driven out when they are dismantled
options.B: Of uniform diameter throughout, fitted in a plain hole to locate two mating parts accurately in position
options.C: Split along its length and opened out after fitting so that a nut on a bolt cannot work loose
options.D: Made hollow and springy so that it grips the sides of a plain drilled hole by its spring action

q: A blind rivet, as used in the fabrication and body work of a workshop, is a rivet:

options.A: Whose head is formed on both sides of the joint by hammering in the ordinary way
options.B: Whose shank is hollow throughout and whose tail is rolled over a washer to close the joint
options.C: Which can be set entirely from the side from which it is inserted, a stem being pulled through it to form the closing head on the far side where access is not possible
options.D: Whose tail is split into legs which are splayed out in soft material such as leather or fibre board

q: Ring oiling, as used for the bearings of workshop machines, is a method of lubrication in which:

options.A: Dippers fitted to a moving part splash oil from a trough over the bearings and gears as the machine runs
options.B: A loose ring riding on the journal dips into an oil sump below and, as the shaft turns, carries oil up continuously to the bearing surface
options.C: Oil is drawn slowly down a wick from a small reservoir and fed drop by drop on to the bearing
options.D: Oil is delivered to all the bearings of a machine under pressure by a pump driven by the machine

q: A steam trap fitted on the steam pipes and equipment of a workshop is a fitting which:

options.A: Opens automatically to let steam escape whenever the pressure in the boiler rises above the safe limit
options.B: Melts and blows out whenever the water in a boiler furnace crown falls dangerously low
options.C: Is opened by hand at intervals to drain water and sludge from the bottom of a boiler
options.D: Lets condensed water and air escape from steam pipes and equipment automatically while preventing live steam from escaping with them

q: A screw jack, as used for lifting work in a workshop, is a lifting device in which:

options.A: The load is raised by turning a screw working in a fixed nut, the thread also holding the load at the height reached
options.B: The load is raised on a ram pushed up by oil pumped into a cylinder by hand
options.C: The load is raised by a chain drawn over a toothed wheel by an endless hand chain
options.D: The load is raised by a toothed rack driven by a pinion turned through a lever

q: Predictive maintenance of the machines of a workshop means maintenance which is:

options.A: Carried out only after a machine has broken down and stopped production
options.B: Carried out on all machines at fixed intervals laid down in a schedule, whether they need it or not
options.C: Planned from the monitored condition of a machine, the machine being taken up for attention when measurements such as vibration show deterioration, before a breakdown occurs
options.D: Carried out by the operators of the machines themselves as part of their daily cleaning and inspection duties

q: Absorption costing, as a method of costing applied to the products of a workshop, is the method in which:

options.A: Only the variable manufacturing costs are charged to the products, the fixed overheads being written off against the period
options.B: Both fixed and variable manufacturing overheads are absorbed into the cost of the products made
options.C: The same costing principles and methods are followed by all the workshops of an undertaking so that their costs can be compared
options.D: Costs are collected for each separate contract undertaken and the profit or loss on each contract is found

q: In costing, a product cost, as the term is applied to the outturn of a workshop, is a cost which:

options.A: Can no longer be recovered because the money has already been spent on a job that is finished
options.B: Is charged notionally in the cost accounts although no actual payment is made for it
options.C: Consists only of the labour and the expenses of converting material into the finished article
options.D: Is identified with the products made and is carried forward in the value of stock until the products are sold

q: In costing, a period cost, as the term is used in connection with a workshop, is a cost which:

options.A: Is charged against the revenue of the period in which it is incurred, instead of being carried forward in the value of stock
options.B: Is worked out in advance from specifications and estimates before production is begun
options.C: Consists of the direct material, the direct labour and the direct expenses of a job added together
options.D: Is the cost that would be given up by using a machine on one job instead of on the best alternative job

q: In costing, an avoidable cost, as the term is used in the decisions taken about a workshop, is a cost which:

options.A: Has already been incurred and cannot be recovered whatever decision is now taken
options.B: Is shared between several products or shops and cannot be traced to any one of them directly
options.C: Will cease to be incurred if a particular activity, product or section is given up or changed
options.D: Has not yet been spent but to which the undertaking is already committed by a decision taken earlier

q: The economic order quantity for an item of material bought for a workshop means:

options.A: The stock level of the item at which a fresh order for the item must be placed
options.B: The size of a purchase order at which the cost of placing orders and the cost of holding stock together are kept at their lowest
options.C: The largest quantity of the item that should be held in stock at any time
options.D: The average quantity of the item held in stock over a full period of consumption

q: Safety stock of an item of material held for the work of a workshop means:

options.A: Stock of the item which has lain unused beyond its expected life and is awaiting disposal
options.B: Stock of the item which is in excess of the quantity required for the programme in hand
options.C: Material of the item which has already been issued to jobs and is lying in the shops as work in progress
options.D: Stock held in reserve over and above the quantity expected to be used, to guard production against delayed supplies or a sudden rise in demand

q: The shrinkage allowance provided on a pattern prepared in the pattern shop of a workshop is the allowance given by:

options.A: Making the vertical faces of the pattern slightly tapered so that it can be withdrawn from the mould
options.B: Making the pattern slightly larger than the casting required, so as to compensate for the contraction of the metal on cooling and solidifying
options.C: Making the pattern slightly larger on the faces which are to be machined after casting
options.D: Making the pattern slightly loose in the mould so that it can be rapped before withdrawal

q: The draft allowance provided on a pattern prepared in the pattern shop of a workshop consists of:

options.A: Extra metal left on the casting for removal by machining
options.B: Extra size given to the pattern to allow for the shrinkage of the casting
options.C: A slight taper given to the vertical faces of the pattern so that it can be withdrawn from the mould without damaging the mould
options.D: A coating of parting sand applied on the face of the pattern

q: A marking gauge, as used in the pattern shop and fitting work of a workshop, is a tool employed for:

options.A: Scribing lines parallel to a prepared edge of the work, at a set distance from that edge
options.B: Measuring the thickness of a sheet or the diameter of a wire
options.C: Checking the squareness of the faces of a component
options.D: Marking the centres of holes to be drilled on a component

q: A limit gauge, as used in the inspection section of a workshop, is a fixed gauge which is used for:

options.A: Measuring the exact size of a dimension of a component
options.B: Marking out the limits of machining on a component
options.C: Setting the measuring instruments of the inspection section
options.D: Checking whether a dimension of a component lies within its prescribed limits, without measuring its actual size

q: Ductile iron, as a material handled in a workshop, is a cast iron which is distinguished in that:

options.A: Its graphite is present in the form of thin flakes, as in ordinary grey iron
options.B: Its graphite is present in spheroidal or nodular form, which gives the iron appreciable ductility and toughness
options.C: It contains practically no carbon at all
options.D: It is produced by prolonged heating of white cast iron in contact with an oxidising medium

q: Phosphor bronze, used in a workshop for worm wheels, bearings and similar components, is an alloy consisting essentially of:

options.A: Copper and tin, with a small addition of phosphorus
options.B: Copper and zinc, with a small addition of lead
options.C: Copper and aluminium, with a small addition of iron
options.D: Tin and lead, with a small addition of antimony

q: Ferrite, as the term is used for the structure of steels handled in a workshop, is the constituent which is:

options.A: The hard compound of iron and carbon present in steel
options.B: The layered mixture formed on the slow cooling of steel
options.C: Iron in an almost pure form, which is soft and ductile in nature
options.D: The structure formed when steel is quenched suddenly from a high temperature

q: Pearlite, as the term is used for the structure of steels handled in a workshop, is the constituent which consists of:

options.A: Pure iron containing practically no carbon
options.B: A hard compound of iron and carbon alone
options.C: The solid solution formed in steel at high temperatures only
options.D: A layered mixture of ferrite and cementite, formed on the slow cooling of steel

q: Martempering of a steel component in the heat treatment shop of a workshop is an interrupted quenching treatment in which the heated component is:

options.A: Quenched into a hot bath, held there until its temperature becomes uniform throughout, and then cooled in air so that martensite forms with reduced distortion and cracking
options.B: Quenched in water and immediately reheated to a moderate temperature to reduce its hardness
options.C: Cooled slowly in the furnace itself after heating
options.D: Heated and cooled repeatedly until the required hardness is obtained

q: Patenting, as carried out in the heat treatment work of a workshop, is a treatment which is applied mainly to:

options.A: Large castings, to relieve the stresses set up in casting
options.B: Steel wire, to give it a structure suitable for further drawing into finer sizes
options.C: Cutting tools, to give them a hard and wear-resistant surface
options.D: Springs, to restore their elasticity after long use

q: A counterbore, as produced on a holed component in a workshop, is:

options.A: A conical enlargement made at the mouth of a hole to receive a countersunk screw head
options.B: A smooth and accurate finish given to the inside of a hole
options.C: A tapered hole made at the mouth of a drilled hole for starting a tap
options.D: A flat-bottomed enlargement at the top of a hole, made to seat the head of a bolt, a nut or a washer below the surface

q: Flank wear, as the term is used for the cutting tools of a workshop, means the wear which takes place:

options.A: On the face of the tool, forming a depression behind the cutting edge
options.B: On the shank of the tool, where it is held in the tool holder
options.C: On the flank or clearance face of the tool, below the cutting edge, through rubbing against the work
options.D: On the nose of the tool only, through sudden impact at the start of the cut

q: The emulsion commonly used as a cutting fluid in the machine shops of a workshop is:

options.A: A soluble oil mixed with water, forming a milky fluid used mainly for cooling the tool and the work
options.B: A neat mineral oil used without any admixture of water
options.C: An oil to which sulphur has been added to improve its cutting action
options.D: A paste of grease and abrasive powder used for lapping work

q: Nibbling, as carried out on sheet metal in a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Folding the edge of a sheet back on itself to stiffen it
options.B: Cutting a sheet along a required outline by a series of small repeated punching cuts
options.C: Stretching a flat sheet into a hollow shape over a former
options.D: Joining the edges of a sheet by hooking them together and pressing them flat

q: Planishing, as carried out in the sheet-metal work of a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Cutting a sheet to the required shape with hand shears
options.B: Bending a sheet along a straight line in a folding machine
options.C: Forming a sheet into a hollow vessel by hammering it over a stake
options.D: Smoothing and finishing the surface of sheet-metal work by hammering or rolling it with smooth tools, so as to remove small irregularities

q: A grooved seam, as made in the sheet-metal work of a workshop, is a seam in which:

options.A: The edges of the sheets are simply overlapped and soldered together
options.B: The edges of the sheets are welded together along the line of the joint
options.C: The edges of the sheets are hooked together and the fold is locked and pressed down with a grooving tool
options.D: The edges of the sheets are held together by rivets passed through both sheets

q: A lap joint, as made in the welding work of a workshop, is a joint in which:

options.A: The parts overlap each other and are welded along the edges of the overlap
options.B: The parts meet edge to edge in the same plane and are welded across the meeting edges
options.C: One part stands upright on the face of the other and is welded at the junction
options.D: The edges of the parts meet at an outer corner and are welded at the corner

q: A T-joint, as made in the welding and fabrication work of a workshop, is a joint in which:

options.A: The parts overlap each other and are welded along the edges of the overlap
options.B: One part is set upright on the face of the other, so that the two form the shape of the letter T, and the junction is welded
options.C: The parts meet edge to edge in the same plane and are welded across the meeting edges
options.D: The edges of the parts are merely placed side by side without any welding

q: Spatter, as the term is used in the welding work of a workshop, means:

options.A: The pool of molten metal formed at the point where the welding is being done
options.B: The coating of slag which forms over the deposited weld metal
options.C: The small globules of molten metal which are thrown out during welding and stick to the surfaces around the joint
options.D: The gas pocket left enclosed within the metal of a finished weld

q: A backfire, as the term is used in gas welding in a workshop, is the occurrence in which:

options.A: The flame travels back continuously through the hose towards the gas cylinder
options.B: The flame leaves the tip of the torch and burns at a distance away from it
options.C: The flame burns inside the nozzle of the torch with a hissing sound
options.D: The flame momentarily returns into the tip of the torch with a popping sound, and either goes out or reappears at the tip

q: A herringbone gear, as used in the drives of workshop machines, is a gear which:

options.A: Has its teeth cut parallel to the axis of the gear
options.B: Is in effect a double helical gear, its teeth being cut in two halves of opposite hand so that the sideways thrust of one half is balanced by that of the other
options.C: Has its teeth cut on the face of the gear instead of on its rim
options.D: Is used for connecting two shafts whose axes do not intersect at all

q: A hypoid gear, as used in the drives of machines and vehicles handled in a workshop, is a gear of the bevel family which is used for connecting:

options.A: Shafts whose axes are offset from each other and do not intersect, the pinion being set to one side of the centre line of the wheel
options.B: Shafts whose axes lie in the same straight line
options.C: Shafts whose axes are parallel to each other
options.D: Shafts whose axes intersect at a right angle and lie in the same plane

q: The pressure angle of the teeth of a gear used in a workshop machine is the angle between:

options.A: The faces of two adjoining teeth of the same gear
options.B: The axis of the gear and the line joining the tips of its teeth
options.C: The direction of the pressure exerted between the teeth in contact and the plane which is tangent to the pitch circles at their point of contact
options.D: The rim of the gear and the spokes by which it is joined to its hub

q: The addendum of the tooth of a gear used in a workshop machine means:

options.A: The radial depth of the tooth below the pitch circle
options.B: The thickness of the tooth measured along the pitch circle
options.C: The whole depth of the tooth from its tip to its root
options.D: The radial height of the tooth above the pitch circle, that is, the distance between the pitch circle and the tip circle

q: A muff coupling, as used to join two shafts in a workshop machine drive, is a coupling which consists of:

options.A: A hollow sleeve fitted over the ends of the two shafts and keyed to both of them
options.B: Two flanges, one keyed to each shaft, bolted together face to face
options.C: A loose pin passing through the ends of the two shafts
options.D: A casing filled with oil, through which the drive is transmitted

q: A fluid coupling, as used in the drives of workshop machines and vehicles, is a coupling which transmits power:

options.A: Through a set of gears enclosed in an oil-tight casing
options.B: Through the oil or other fluid set in motion by the driving member, there being no direct mechanical connection between the driving and the driven members
options.C: Through a friction disc pressed against the face of a flywheel
options.D: Through a chain running over sprockets fitted on the two shafts

q: A knuckle joint, as used for connecting rods in the equipment handled in a workshop, is a joint in which:

options.A: The ends of the two rods are screwed into a common sleeve
options.B: The two rods are welded together at their ends
options.C: The eye end of one rod fits into the forked end of the other and the two are joined by a pin, so that the rods can move angularly in a single plane
options.D: The ends of the two rods are overlapped and riveted together

q: A turnbuckle, as used with the tie rods and stays of the equipment handled in a workshop, is a device which serves to:

options.A: Adjust the tension or the effective length of a tie rod, its body carrying threads of opposite hand at its two ends
options.B: Join two ropes together so that they can be separated quickly
options.C: Hold a load suspended from a crane hook in a fixed position
options.D: Lock a nut in position so that it cannot slacken back in service

q: A cone pulley, as used in the headstock drive of a workshop machine, is a pulley which:

options.A: Is fitted loosely on its shaft so that the drive can be engaged and disengaged at will
options.B: Presses against the side of a belt to keep the belt tight
options.C: Carries the rope of a rope drive in a groove cut around its rim
options.D: Has steps of different diameters formed on it, so that different speeds are obtained by shifting the belt from step to step with the matching pulley

q: A jockey pulley, as used in the belt drives of workshop machines, is a small pulley which:

options.A: Is keyed to the main shaft of the machine and drives the countershaft
options.B: Is mounted loosely so as to press against the belt, increasing its wrap on the driving pulley and keeping it tight
options.C: Is used only for driving a machine in the reverse direction
options.D: Carries the belt across from one machine to another at a distance

q: A rope drive, as used for transmitting power in and around a workshop, is a drive in which:

options.A: Power is transmitted by a flat leather belt running on flat pulleys
options.B: Power is transmitted by a toothed belt running on toothed pulleys
options.C: Power is transmitted by ropes running in grooves on the rims of the pulleys, and it is suited to transmitting large power over considerable distances
options.D: Power is transmitted by a chain running over toothed sprockets

q: An eye bolt, as used in the lifting and erection work of a workshop, is a bolt which:

options.A: Has a hexagonal head tightened by means of a spanner in the ordinary way
options.B: Is bent at its end into the form of a hook
options.C: Is screwed into the ground to anchor a machine to its foundation
options.D: Has its head formed into a closed ring or eye, through which a lifting hook or shackle can be passed

q: An acorn nut, as used on the equipment and assemblies of a workshop, is a nut which:

options.A: Is closed at its outer end by a dome-shaped cap, so that it covers and protects the projecting end of the bolt
options.B: Is provided with projecting lugs by which it can be tightened by hand
options.C: Has slots cut across its top so that it can be locked by a split pin
options.D: Is made square in shape so that it can be held in a recess without a spanner

q: A spring pin, as used in the assembly work of a workshop, is a pin which:

options.A: Is threaded along its whole length so that it can be screwed into position
options.B: Is hollow and slit along its length, and being slightly larger than its hole it grips the hole firmly by its spring action when driven in
options.C: Is tapered along its length and is driven in to locate two parts together
options.D: Is bent at one end after insertion so that it cannot work out of its hole

q: Under the first in, first out method of pricing material issued from a workshop store, the material issued is priced at:

options.A: The price of the latest lot received into the store
options.B: The average price of all the lots held in the store
options.C: The price of the earliest lot still held in the store, the lots being treated as issued in the order in which they were received
options.D: The price expected to be paid for replacing the material issued

q: The re-order level of an item of material held for the work of a workshop is the level of stock at which:

options.A: The stock of the item is completely exhausted
options.B: Emergency purchases of the item have to be made at once
options.C: The issue of the item from the store has to be stopped
options.D: A fresh order for the purchase of the item is placed, so that the new supply arrives before the existing stock is exhausted

q: The danger level of an item of material held for the work of a workshop is the level:

options.A: Below which the stock of the item is not normally allowed to fall, special and emergency action being taken to obtain supplies when it is reached
options.B: At which a fresh order for the purchase of the item is placed in the ordinary course
options.C: Above which the stock of the item is not allowed to rise at any time
options.D: At which the item is declared as surplus to the requirements of the workshop

q: Under the two-bin system of controlling the material held for the work of a workshop, the stock of an item is:

options.A: Kept under lock in two separate stores for reasons of safety
options.B: Kept in two bins or lots, material being drawn from one of them and a fresh order being placed when that lot is exhausted, the second lot being used while the supply is awaited
options.C: Priced by two different methods in alternate months
options.D: Verified physically twice in the course of every year

q: In costing, a committed cost, as the term is used in connection with a workshop, is a cost which:

options.A: Is incurred only when a particular job is taken up in the workshop
options.B: Can be avoided altogether by stopping a particular line of work
options.C: Arises from decisions and commitments already made, such as the rent of the premises and the charges on plant already acquired, and cannot be altered readily in the short run
options.D: Is not recorded in the books at all and is brought in only for purposes of comparison

q: A gate valve, as fitted on the steam and water pipes of a workshop, is a valve in which:

options.A: The flow is regulated by a disc which is screwed down on to a seat across the passage
options.B: The flow is allowed in one direction only and is stopped automatically on reversal
options.C: A ball with a passage through it is turned to open or close the flow
options.D: A gate or slide is raised clear of the passage to give a full opening, the valve being suited to being either fully open or fully closed rather than to regulating the flow

q: A globe valve, as fitted on the steam and water pipes of a workshop, is a valve which is distinguished in that:

options.A: The flow passes through a seat on which a disc is screwed down, the passage being turned in its course, so that the valve is suited to regulating or throttling the flow
options.B: A gate is raised clear of the passage to give a full and unobstructed opening
options.C: The flow is allowed in one direction only and is stopped automatically on reversal
options.D: It is fitted at the foot of a suction pipe to retain the water in the pipe

q: A check valve, as fitted on the pipes and equipment of a workshop, is a valve which:

options.A: Is opened and closed by hand by means of a handwheel
options.B: Allows the flow in one direction only and closes automatically when the flow tries to reverse
options.C: Opens automatically to release the pressure when it rises beyond a safe limit
options.D: Is used for draining out the water collected in a pipe or vessel

q: A foot valve, as fitted on the pumping equipment of a workshop, is a valve which is:

options.A: Operated by the foot of the attendant instead of by a handwheel
options.B: Fitted on the delivery pipe of a pump to regulate the quantity delivered
options.C: A check valve fitted at the bottom end of the suction pipe of a pump, which retains the water in the pipe and so keeps the pump primed
options.D: Fitted on a steam pipe to discharge the water of condensation automatically

q: The Bourdon tube, as used in the pressure gauges fitted on the boilers and pipes of a workshop, is the part of the gauge which:

options.A: Contains the liquid whose level shows the pressure in the vessel
options.B: Protects the glass of the gauge from damage by steam and water
options.C: Connects the gauge to the boiler and isolates it from vibration
options.D: Is a curved tube of oval section which tends to straighten as the pressure inside it rises, and so moves the pointer of the gauge

q: Cavitation, as the term is used for the pumps and hydraulic equipment handled in a workshop, is the phenomenon in which:

options.A: Vapour bubbles form in a liquid where its pressure falls and then collapse violently where the pressure rises again, damaging the surfaces of impellers and casings
options.B: Air is drawn into a pump along with the liquid because of a leaking suction joint
options.C: The liquid in a pipe is set in motion in the reverse direction when a valve is closed
options.D: A liquid hammering sound is produced in a steam pipe by the water of condensation collected in it

q: A flat file used by fitters in a workshop is a file which:

options.A: Is triangular in cross-section and is used for filing sharp corners and angles
options.B: Is rectangular in cross-section and is the file commonly used for general filing of flat surfaces
options.C: Is round in cross-section and is used for enlarging round holes
options.D: Is curved on both of its faces and is used only on concave surfaces

q: A half-round file used in the fitting shop of a workshop is a file which:

options.A: Has one flat face and one convex (rounded) face, so that it can be used on flat as well as curved surfaces
options.B: Has both of its faces convex and rounded
options.C: Has both of its faces flat and parallel
options.D: Is triangular in cross-section, like a saw file

q: Combination pliers, as used by fitters and electricians in a workshop, are pliers which:

options.A: Are used only for cutting wires and cables
options.B: Are used only for turning nuts on bolts
options.C: Combine flat gripping jaws, a pipe grip and a wire-cutting edge in one tool, for gripping, bending and cutting
options.D: Are used for holding hot metal in the smithy

q: An adjustable spanner, as used in the fitting and maintenance work of a workshop, is a spanner in which:

options.A: Both ends carry fixed open jaws of different sizes
options.B: A ring completely encloses the nut on all sides
options.C: The jaw is in the form of a socket fitted on a handle
options.D: The opening of the jaw can be varied by a worm screw, so that one spanner suits a range of nut sizes

q: A soft hammer (soft-faced hammer) used in the assembly and fitting work of a workshop is a hammer which:

options.A: Has a head of copper, rawhide, plastic or similar soft material, so that it can strike finished parts without damaging their surfaces
options.B: Has a head of hardened steel and is used for riveting work
options.C: Is a heavy hammer used for breaking stone and concrete
options.D: Is used for driving spikes and large nails in timber work

q: A faceplate, as used on a centre lathe in a workshop, is a device which:

options.A: Is a small disc used for holding only round bars between centres
options.B: Is the plate on which the lathe bed is mounted
options.C: Is a large slotted disc fitted to the spindle nose, on which work too irregular to be held in a chuck or between centres is clamped for turning
options.D: Is a cover plate fitted over the headstock gears

q: The clapper box fitted on the tool head of a shaping machine in a workshop is the part which:

options.A: Holds the workpiece firmly on the machine table
options.B: Holds the cutting tool and is hinged so that the tool lifts slightly on the return stroke instead of dragging over the work
options.C: Converts the rotary motion of the motor into reciprocating motion
options.D: Is used for setting the length of the stroke of the machine

q: A drill sleeve, as used with the drilling machines of a workshop, is a tapered sleeve which is used:

options.A: For holding a straight-shank drill in the machine spindle
options.B: For increasing the size of a hole already drilled
options.C: As an extension to reach holes in deep recesses
options.D: To fit a drill whose taper shank is smaller than the taper bore of the machine spindle

q: The helix angle of a twist drill used in a workshop is the angle:

options.A: Which the helical flute of the drill makes with the axis of the drill
options.B: Between the two cutting lips at the point of the drill
options.C: Between the face of the land and the tangent to the drill surface
options.D: Of relief provided behind the cutting edge of the drill

q: The chisel edge of a twist drill used in a workshop is the edge which:

options.A: Runs along the whole length of the flute of the drill
options.B: Is formed at the outer corner of each cutting lip
options.C: Is the short edge at the centre of the drill point, formed by the meeting of the two flank faces and joining the two cutting lips
options.D: Is ground on the margin of the drill for guiding it in the hole

q: Parallels, as used in the machine shops of a workshop, are:

options.A: Bars fitted in the slots of the machine table for clamping work
options.B: Pairs of hardened steel strips of accurately equal height, placed under work to raise it and keep it level and parallel with the machine table
options.C: Straight edges used for testing the flatness of surfaces
options.D: Gauges used for checking the parallelism of two shafts

q: A rotary table, as used on a milling machine in a workshop, is a table which:

options.A: Only reciprocates in a straight line under the cutter
options.B: Raises and lowers the work for setting the depth of cut
options.C: Tilts the work to any required angle in a vertical plane
options.D: Holds the work flat and can be rotated by a graduated hand wheel, so that circular arcs and equally spaced features can be milled

q: A square thread, as used on the screws of workshop machines and equipment, is a thread in which:

options.A: The flanks of the thread are at right angles to its axis, and it is used for transmitting power, as in screw jacks, vices and presses
options.B: The thread has a V profile and is used for ordinary fastening work
options.C: The flanks are inclined and the top of the thread is flat, as in an Acme thread
options.D: The thread is rounded at the top and bottom, as in a knuckle thread

q: A buttress thread, as used on the screws of workshop equipment, is a thread which:

options.A: Is used only for fastening purposes on pipes
options.B: Can take heavy load equally in both directions along the axis
options.C: Has one flank nearly at right angles to the axis and the other flank inclined, so that it takes heavy load mainly in one direction
options.D: Has a rounded profile and is used on bottle caps and lamp holders

q: The dedendum of the tooth of a gear used in a workshop machine is:

options.A: The height of the tooth above the pitch circle
options.B: The radial depth of the tooth below the pitch circle, measured from the pitch circle to the bottom of the tooth space
options.C: The whole depth of the tooth from its top to its root
options.D: The thickness of the tooth measured on the pitch circle

q: The circular pitch of a gear used in a workshop machine is:

options.A: The distance between the centres of two meshing gears
options.B: The thickness of a tooth measured at the root circle
options.C: The diameter of the pitch circle divided by the number of teeth
options.D: The distance, measured along the pitch circle, from a point on one tooth to the corresponding point on the next tooth

q: An internal gear, as used in the drives of workshop machines, is a gear:

options.A: Whose teeth are cut on the inside surface of a ring, and which meshes with an external pinion placed inside it
options.B: Which is completely enclosed inside the housing of a machine
options.C: Whose teeth are cut on the face of a disc at right angles to its axis
options.D: Which has no teeth and drives the mating gear by friction alone

q: An idler gear in a gear train of a workshop machine is a gear which:

options.A: Runs freely on its shaft without transmitting any power
options.B: Is the smallest gear of the train and fixes the gear ratio
options.C: Is placed between the driving and the driven gear to connect them and to obtain the required direction of rotation, without changing the magnitude of the velocity ratio
options.D: Is used only for reversing the direction of the driven shaft by hand

q: In an epicyclic (planetary) gear train, as used in workshop machines and equipment:

options.A: All the gears rotate about fixed axes only
options.B: One or more gears, called planets, rotate about their own axes while also revolving round a central sun gear, their axes being carried by a moving arm or carrier
options.C: The gears slide along their shafts to change the speed ratio
options.D: Power is transmitted from one gear to another only through a belt

q: A cone clutch, as used in the drives of workshop machines, is a clutch in which:

options.A: Interlocking jaws on the two halves engage with each other
options.B: Shoes are thrown outwards by centrifugal force to engage a drum
options.C: The two halves are drawn together by an electromagnet
options.D: The engaging friction surfaces are conical in shape, the cone form giving a strong wedging action
